utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Very good morning to everybody. May we first hear the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is case number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may we hear the appearances of day 65?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, good morning to you. Kapila Waidyaratne with my colleagues Nicholas Koumjian and Ruth Karper appearing for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Branko Lukic, John Ostojic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you, please, to proceed with the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you get enough rest?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will not take long today. We just have several minor points to clarify, and then I will, in a manner of speaking, hand you over to the Trial Chamber. Did you have the impression that the preparations that were taking place in Kozarac to defend Kozarac were part of a wider plan?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no such impression. In Kozarac there could not have been any wider plan. Everybody was about Kozarac itself because Kozarac was not physically connected with a wider area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in the meetings held in Kozarac, persons from other regions also participated? Such as Kemal Alagic, nicknamed Divljak?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Kemal Alagic, also known as Divljak, with his group, took part in an attempt to take Kozarac back?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina reported by the Minister of the Interior, Alija Delimustafic, and sent by him to all public security centres and public security stations to put up roadblocks on all roads throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, which the JNA were using to evacuate the military and technical equipment?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that. First thing I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you something about your father. The certificate he was issued by the civilian authorities, that he could move about freely after he had been released from one of the camps, you say that when he showed this certificate to the soldiers, they told him in a rude way that they would not recognise that certificate.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually that was a certificate he had obtained from the Serbian Red Cross in Trnopolje and that certificate only permitted him to go with his family to the next village and that he could continue to live at my grandfather's place, my mother's father's place. When the soldiers knocked at his door, he produced the certificate hoping that he would thereby prove that he was -- that he had been legally released from the camp but they just cut the certificate up, they tore it up, and they took him away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Sead Cirkin, ex-JNA captain, is still alive today?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did see him in the Keraterm camp during your detention there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Kozarac prior to the breakout of the conflict, were you familiar with the existence of such groups as Kole's group or Ramiz's group?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to know both Kole and Ramiz, not very well but I did not know anything about any groups related to them. Those were not people I was spending much of my time with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you not by any chance hear from other people that they were organising military groups?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to see Kole in Kozarac during that period but whether he was organising any groups, I couldn't tell. There are always people whom one decides to spend more time with than other people one just knows but does not spend much time with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you a member of the Territorial Defence of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the period after the general call-up by the government in Sarajevo, and the mobilisation, well, yes, in that case, I did it take part as a citizen who tried to protect his family. But I was not a member of any uniformed unit wearing any sort of insignia or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you sign up to become a member of the Kozarac TO?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness the document marked as D11? And to show him page A/1/90?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the ELMO, you can see a page which is part of a document listing all members of the Kozarac TO. Under number 92, we can see the name Jusuf Arifagic. I would now like to ask the usher to please show the witness the statement given by him on the 21st and 22nd October, 1994, to the investigators of the Tribunal. This is your own statement from 1994. It's in English, and what we need this statement for now is for you to tell us whether, at the bottom of the page, there is your signature?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you also recognise the signature next to the name Jusuf Arifagic under number 92 as your own signature also?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you now recall the fact that in fact you signed up to become a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us, this had nothing to do with membership of the TO. This was just a list of persons who took part in the guard duty around Kozarac. So this is not a full list of TO members. This is a different thing. I know that I signed down on a list containing the names of people who stood guard around Kozarac. In any sense of active service, wearing uniform, commanding or anything like that, I was not a member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please put the document D11 back on the ELMO? And could you just pull it up a bit higher so that we can see the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The bottom of the page, there is typewritten "the TO staff of Kozarac".

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think when these lists were drawn up, we just signed. I don't think they were even typewritten. I know that lists of people were made who would stand guard around Kozarac. This TO and the rest, when it was added I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say you signed this without the names being typewritten?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's possible. We just put our name down as people who would stand guard around Kozarac. What was done with these lists later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doesn't it seem obvious to you that first the names were typewritten and then the lines were drawn because the lines were added after the names had been typewritten obviously?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, usher, we no longer require this document. May I just have a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the attack began on the 24th of May, 1992, the attack against the guard post at which you were, we explained yesterday how you gave instructions to the people there to shoot in pairs, two by two. However, I forgot to ask you -- you then continued and that's on page 6, paragraph 4, of your statement from 1994, B/C/S version, in the English version page 6, paragraph 6, the last two sentences: "This continued for about ten to 15 minutes. The Serbs at our defence line then withdrew into Balte proper." Does this mean that, at first, you were able to repulse the attack by the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may be a mistranslation. There was no attack and thee was no combat there, but I think this needs to be connected with the fighting in Jakupovici because after the attack began, the attacks which were coming from Balte and Jankovici, we were told that we had enough time to evacuate and that area was about to fall and people were starting to withdraw towards the centre of Kozarac so that's what the whole situation was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you were able to hold them at bay for a while and even repulse them back?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually we were not holding them at bay. We had just opened fire and we simulated the firing, the attack. We thought that they would perhaps withdraw. This turned out to be true, and the people in Kamicani, for instance, the civilians there, had enough time to withdraw towards the centre of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 6, paragraph 6 of the B/C/S version of your statement, given the same year, or page 6, paragraph 8 of the English version of this statement, you make mention of a motel or a hospital in the forest by which you passed on the 26th of May, 1992, about noon, with the intention to contact Captain Cirkin. Do you know by any chance when this motel was converted into a hospital? When did this become a makeshift hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was never converted into a hospital. It was simply a facility which was away from Kozarac in the direction of Mrakovica, not far from the last village in the outskirts of Kozarac. It was located towards the forest. It was not actually finished and the people who were wounded were taken there. Also, the patients from the local hospital, the health centre in Kozarac, they were transferred there, together with the equipment that they were able to take from the hospital. It was never really converted into a hospital. It was not possible to receive any kind of proper treatment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the medical supplies were initially taken to this facility with the purpose of using them there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When Captain Cirkin issued his order to the person manning the checkpoint that he should let the tanks come close enough so that they could destroy them with zoljas, is it true that prior to that, he had said that things should finally start, that there can no longer be any stalling?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us try to clear up one more issue concerning Keraterm and I will try to complete my cross-examination after that. I am referring to the night of the massacre in Room 3 in Keraterm. Do you know whose shift was on duty on that night?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, it was Kole's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Simo Drljaca arrive after the first day or the second day?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was after the second massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long were the shifts in Keraterm, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they lasted 12 hours. They would start in the morning and last until the evening and then there would be the following shift starting in the evening and until the morning. We were not familiar with the way it worked and how the guards were rotated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whose shift was on duty on the second night, the night of the second massacre?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing. In your statement you said that when you were transferred, when you were taken to the Prijedor hospital from Keraterm after you had been badly beaten, you were admitted and treated by a Bosniak doctor. Do you know what his name is?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just stated in my statement that on the way to hospital, we encountered a doctor of Bosniak ethnicity. We talked briefly and then he left. After that, we were taken to the surgery department, at least I think it was the surgery department. I was taken care of by a nurse. She helped me as much as she was able to help me, and we also briefly spoke to another doctor who worked in this hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know his name. It happened at the entrance to the hospital, in the corridor. It was a very brief conversation. He didn't dare talk to us very long, and we continued on our way after this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for having answered my questions. I wish you all the best in the future, wherever you may be.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to come back to about five issues where some clarity still is needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I beg your pardon already in advance if I missed something during your statement. I recollect that on page 47 of your statement, you described the story of your father being brought to the camp, first to Trnopolje, then to Keraterm, and then page 47, this story ends at line 19, when you confirmed that your father was retransferred to the Trnopolje camp again. Could you please tell us about the fate of your father after this retransfer to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this retransfer to Trnopolje, as he was leaving Trnopolje, and this is the reason maybe why I need to give you a longer explanation, this was actually the departure between a father and a son, he didn't know where he would go. He didn't know about the fate of his other son, and I wanted to tell him that if -- that he should try and find my wife and my children once he reaches the free territory, which is what he did. And after he arrived in Slovenia as a refugee, he underwent a surgery which he had to undergo as a result of the beating he had sustained in the camp. It was a surgery in the nose area. It didn't really work well so he had to do another one. He's not a very healthy person. If the weather is bad, his health condition is such that he experiences severe problems. The doctors told him that he should install an alarm at home in case he runs out of breath or has any problems. But we, his children, are trying to do our best to take care of him. But he is a disabled person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. A second issue is related to Keraterm. In your testimony of 1994, page 22, first paragraph, I quote a full paragraph. You said the following: "I remember about two nights after the second shooting in Room 3, Kajin came to the front of room 2 and was standing squeezing the bars with his hands. He was drunk and he was crying. He told us that the shootings had been in retaliation for what occurred in World War II. He also told us that one or two Serb soldiers were killed in Hambarine and that was another reason for the shootings. He told us that he did not agree with Chetnik politics, he had lost many of his friends and he then threw his pistol away. A number of guards then came and took him away." The first question is: Is this also your testimony of today?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what he said. And this is what I emphasised in my previous testimony and in my statement. He did not wish to torture people. He was in favour of fair trials. I don't know why I remember this to this date. I liked him for that. I liked what he said, because of all the torture that he had sustained and this is exactly what he said. I have reported his exact words. He was drunk. He was crying. And the large number of people in Room 3 were people whom he knew very well. The guard who came and tried to take him away didn't manage to. He continued talking and eventually he discarded his pistol and was finally taken away by others. I think that many people in room 1 were also able to hear this. It was not very far from them as well. Those were his word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Kajin later?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, during my detention, of course, we saw him from time to time in the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In the years after your detention in the camp, did you ever meet him again?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, in the courtroom. First time after my detention in the camp, and his service there as a guard, we met him -- I met him here for the first time in a proceedings against him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this additional confirmation. Then I have to turn to the question of the helicopters coming in. It's a twofold question. In your testimony of 1994, page 3, last paragraph and page 4, first paragraph, you stated the following: "On one occasion, I saw a helicopter land in Balte. Balte is about one kilometre from my home. I cannot recall the date but it was between 10 p.m. and 11 p.m. I first heard the helicopter and then I saw it in the air and shortly after, saw it landing near the house of Duro Kozomara, a Serb." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "He was active in the SDS but I'm unaware what function he held. I heard the engine being cut. I did not pay any more attention to the helicopter. This was the only occasion I saw a helicopter in Balte." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then let's turn to -- I'm afraid the question was still open after the examination and the cross-examination -- page 3, second-last paragraph, you stated in 1994, "In February or March, 1992, I saw and heard helicopters in the air during the night around Kozarac. It was very rare for helicopters to be in this area during the night. I heard the helicopters on almost nightly basis. I never saw a helicopter land in Kozarac but it is my belief that they landed in Serb villages surrounding Kozarac. I did not see any emblems on the helicopters and I am unable to say for what they were being used." This is your written statement in English. Please understand that I have to ask you how do you yourself regard it as possible that during your testimony yesterday, you were able to tell us that in these helicopters, there were weapons and weapons were unloaded? Yes, please, first of all try yourself to find an explanation for this distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two aspects of the issue. There were frequent flights of helicopters in this area. The military activity generally speaking had intensified and then in the second part of this portion of my statement, I was referring to a helicopter that I saw landing in the village of Balte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. But wouldn't you agree that it would be normal that if you saw, indeed, that in the helicopters there were weapons and weapons were unloaded, that at that time you would have mentioned this instead of saying, in general that you are unable to say for what they were being used?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that I had directly seen weapons being unloaded. In order to reach the village of Balte, you have to pass through the entire town of Kozarac and Muslim villages. No one ever observed any convoy of vehicles or trucks carrying weapons in the direction of Balte. However, when the attack on Kozarac started from the direction of the village of Balte, the fire that was opened was mortar fire and fire opened from various kinds of infantry weapons which means that those weapons could reach Balte only by helicopter, not by land, and in my statement that I gave after the war, I said that those helicopters had brought the weapons in Balte and had armed the population, the Serb population in Balte, including the one that I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. And then finally, I'm fully aware that already yesterday the Prosecutor asked you several times about names of persons being responsible in the area of Kozarac, Prijedor, and you mentioned names of Mr. Drljaca, Kovacevic and others. Now to start the other way around, just to be quite clear and on the safe side, for the transcript, did you ever before the 30th of April or later in 1992, have heard the name of Dr. Stakic, being in his capacity of a physician or in another capacity?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other questions? Judge Fassi Fihri? Judge Vassylenko? No, are there any additional questions emanating from this line of questions of the judges or any questions by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is not the case. Then I have to thank you for all your efforts, not only for coming here, for also answering our questions patiently and it's also for the judges to wish you all the best and to try to overcome as soon as, and as far as it is possible, that what you have experienced at that time, and we all hope that this can be one small brick in the wall building up a better and safer society in your home country. Thank you. You are excused finally for this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the Office of the Prosecutor has offered us now a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I promised that, but it turns out that the video, the -- in order to get a good quality of those 15 minutes to get copies for the Court, it will not be ready today. Possibly this afternoon. As I mentioned to the legal officer this morning, we have some severe scheduling problems I'd like to discuss with both the Defence and the court, particularly regarding the translations of expert reports and I would request a conference on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This request for a 65 ter conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, also Mr. Inayat, we can address this at the conference but while he's here and is available and we have the lists available that he can testify to the sourcing, ideally, it was my intent to have one document prepared covering all of the exhibits, rather than the six lists which also do not cover, I think, a few documents that were obtained from witnesses outside of the lists but that would not be ready today. So we can discuss it at the conference what would be the best time for him to testify. He's available to testify today but we have problems next week also with getting witnesses, which I will explain to you. We may have holes in the schedule next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No good news but let's face the problem immediately. What is the most appropriate to have the 65 ter conference in this courtroom? Can you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My preference would be to do it in chambers, and also the Defence. I think the informality would aid the resolution of some of the issues and I also would like to have, ask one investigator to be present who has been doing the scheduling of witnesses and she can explain, and I'd also rather not do that publicly. She can explain some of the problems various witnesses have in altering their schedule. One of the problems is that at the end of the case we are very, very limited in our choices of our witnesses and those remaining generally have scheduling problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Fine. How can we then proceed? Could we meet in my office at 11.00 sharp and I would ask for the presence of two French interpreters, because, no doubt, it will take us longer than half an hour. But then we should try to use -- to make use of the afternoon, and let's try to do as if it would be an ordinary day. This would mean that we could restart at 2.00. I am myself surprised by this development, therefore I would ask all the other participants, also the interpreters to protest immediately if there are some obstacles when we restart, say, at 2.00 and then proceed until 4.30 or 5.00. I think we have numerous problems we can resolve only in courtroom. It's difficult to look through the glass. Okay? I can see no open protest.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: English interpretation says okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then let's proceed this way. 11.00 sharp in my office, as a formal 65 ter meeting in the presence of the representative of the Registry and then the trial stays, as such, stays adjourned until 2.00 sharp. --- Break taken at 10.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's a long time ago. I think it was the 1st of August, 2002, Witness Sivac gave us the entire video, and it is ready to be played now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct. But just for clarification, 15 minutes of the videotape that Mr. Sivac gave us has been copied. As you recall, there was a tape of a trip of a group and other matters that were extraneous with the 15 minutes relevant to events in Prijedor is prepared. I guess the booth has a copy. I'm tendering now the copies for the Court and Defence. And for the record, that's ERN number V0004001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did we attach it already to the one minute and eight seconds an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Shouldn't we maintain the same exhibit number for the entire video or put a -1 to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That would make sense. Also this transcript and video includes the minute and ten seconds or so of the accused speaking. So we could substitute it or we could simply attach it an additional number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's appropriate to give to the video as such -1, and to the transcript -2. Can we start the video?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "REPORTER: People from the Hambarine settlement located five kilometres in the direction of Ljubija held up a vehicle with the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army members. They killed two soldiers and injured four. Rade Lukic and Radovan Milojica were killed and Ratko Milojica and Sinisa Mijatovic were severely injured. The police were prevented from pulling out the dead and injured and the army was forced to open fire without destroying any facilities. SINISA MIJATOVIC: I was sitting with another four comrades of mine at the back seat of the vehicle. Then they cocked the rifle, which he took from them and it fired. Then they opened fire at us from all sides. The slaughter started. Ratko and I somehow managed to get out of the vehicle. I sustained a number of injuries in the arms, legs, and stomach area. Then I was lying behind the car, fearing that the car would explode. They couldn't see that those two were dead, the dead bodies there. They left towards (inaudible) report. REPORTER: Who was firing at you. SINISA MIJATOVIC: The so-called TO of that place was firing. They were mostly Muslims, my school friends. REPORTER: The Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality requested the people from Hambarine to surrender former policeman Aziz Aliskovic and his group, who carried out the attack on soldiers. The twelve o'clock deadline was not observed. Half an hour after the deadline expired the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina launched an artillery attack on Hambarine and cleaned up the area where the Green Berets had been concentrated. The militant wing of the Party for Democratic Action obviously did not wish to preserve peace in Prijedor. SIMO MISKOVIC: There had been interparty agreements prior to this incident and in all talks that were conducted between the SDS and the SDA, the SDS mainly sent a strong message to all party leaderships in the Prijedor municipality reminding them of their obligation and responsibility to take care primarily of this town, these people, and not to leave our children and the descendants with the traumas that were left by our parents. However, the militant wing of the SDA most probably didn't wish this to be implemented and it most likely had its own plans, goals to realise and ambitions that had been realised in Sarajevo, Mostar, Kupres, and so on. They also cautioned that this would not happen in the area of Prijedor, but we have used all possible means, through talks, both party talks and talks with people and prominent citizens, delegations were coming two days before this incident or this conflict. A great number of talks were held in all areas, with Muslim population, with the goal of securing peace in this region and preventing any sort of conflict from breaking out, regardless of solutions which will definitely come about at the level of this local commune. REPORTER: Sunday, May 24th. The reason -- reason has prevailed in many local communes of Prijedor municipality. People are returning illegally acquired weapons, either individually or in an organised manner. The local communes of Donja Puharska, Rizvanovici, Biscani and the village of Rakovcani can confirm this. HAMZA KAPETANOVIC: We are talking about some 4 machine-guns. 50 per cent of the 49 barrels we have are automatic weapons. Those weapons used to belong to the TO and the reserve police force and part of them was acquired by citizens on an individual basis. We were informed today at 10.30 that these weapons ought to be returned to the barracks by 12.00 but the deadline was extended to 1.00 and we collected everything and brought it there. People brought them to the local commune and we brought them here. Ever since this citizens' forum was established in Donja Puharska, after the takeover of power, we have been doing everything in cooperation with the local commune. We haven't done anything. We have even recently kept guard together so nobody is missing a hair in Donja Puharska or in the settlement with Serbian population which is bordering on ours with predominantly Muslim population. DZEVAD KADIRIC: We are in the local commune of Biscani. I am Dzevad Kadiric. REPORTER: I can see you are wearing a military uniform. DZEVAD KADIRIC: I also think so. I don't mind it. REPORTER: Tell us how the collection of weapons went and how many barrels you have brought from the village. DZEVAD KADIRIC: I have brought into the establishment amount I was issued with, ammunition and how shall I put it, rifles and so on. REPORTER: These are all weapons and ammunition of a unit, detachment of the former TO. DZEVAD KADIRIC: The unit, TO platoon, yes, independent platoon of the Biscani local commune which is under the command of the Prijedor municipal Territorial Defence. REPORTER: Can you tell us what the situation like with other weapons? There is information that there is a great number of illegally acquired weapons and military equipment. DZEVAD KADIRIC: What can I tell you? Firstly, I can assure you that the information is not accurate. I cannot guarantee a hundred per cent, nor would I want to, maybe someone does possess a small number of weapons but they are a great minority, and this could only be the case for quite light weapons like pistols and similar, if there is any, but I doubt that there are any heavy weapons in the local commune of Biscani. REPORTER: What is the amount? How many rifles and other weapons have been brought into the barracks, and is that all from all those local communes that were given the ultimatum until yesterday at 1800 hours? CAPTAIN MILAN BARUDZIJA: These are not all the weapons, that is, not from all the local communes. So far 54 rifles with ammunition and other equipment that comes with them have been surrendered from the local communes of Rakovcani and Rizvanovici. However, later, with the arrival of the reserve platoon of the Territorial Defence and the police from the Biscani local commune with the total number of 39 barrels and also with the necessary number of other equipment that comes with these weapons. Donja Puharska representatives have arrived just now, and from them we shall take over the rest. To recapitulate, the total number of weapons that have been surrendered so far is, as I said, 54 rifles from Rakovcani and Rizvanovici and 39 barrels from Biscani. REPORTER: While the handing over of weapons in the Prijedor barracks strengthens optimism, armed conflict has occurred in Kozarac, a settlement 10 kilometres away from Prijedor in the direction of Banja Luka. Infiltrated groups of Green Berets with local extremists obstruct the handover of weapons. Around 1400 hours, fire was opened at the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Hercegovina Army members from the village of Jakupovici. Fighting continues in the afternoon and through the night. Monday, May 25th, severe fighting is going on around Kozarac. Heavy pressure exercised by the Serbian army and artillery fire forces numerous extremists to withdraw. Hundreds of Green Beret members have surrendered in the villages of Donji Jakupovici, Kevljani, Kozarusa, and the surrounding hamlets. The local hodza in Kevljani organised the surrender of all weapons in the village. The villagers were treated very correctly. Serif Velic, from the village of Kevljani. SERIF VELIC: On behalf of the Kevljani local commune I would like to say and stress the fair conduct of these soldiers who have come here. First they distributed bread and pates and then juices to the children and in the end there was military bean stew for the young, women, and children. REPORTER: Word has it that more than 1.000 Green Beret members and their accomplices from the region of the Cazin Krajina and Croatia have gathered in Kozarac proper. They are under the command of Becir Medunjanin, of Albanian origin, whose group is preventing the ceasefire and the surrender of weapons either going into battle or getting a bullet in the head. There is no exact information regarding the losses on the side of the Muslim armed formations but all estimates suggest that casualties are numerous. May 26th, armed formations of the Muslim extremists are completely surrounded. They do not show their willingness to surrender weapons. At night they open sniper fire from Kamicani, Kozarac, Trnopolje, Trnjine. The village of Jakupovici, until yesterday one of the strongest Muslim strongholds, has been mopped up. RADENKO DELIC: The situation after two days of negotiating and persistent talks with them, they still refuse to surrender the weapons. They have requested buses to take out the population, women, and children, which means they are preparing themselves for heavier fighting than so far. REPORTER: [Inaudible] RADENKO DELIC: Women and children are, buses are ready to transfer them. OSTOJA MIODRAG: Muslims should be forced to respect the authority, to respect the more powerful, their own children, because 1941 is long gone. Here along this street a 16-year-old Muslim escorted 50 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people, people who were sent to and killed and slaughtered there. I think that those times shall never come back. My son and the generation of today, you, the young, shall never let anyone persecute you, kill you and slaughter you. REPORTER: Let this statement of Ostoja Miodrag, WWII veteran and a gusle player from Potkozarje, be a message and a lesson. Today, May 27th, fighting still continues in and around Kozarac. Alija Izetbegovic's policy and Zagreb's strong influence, which significantly intensified in this Muslim settlement since political turmoil in Croatia began, have led the population of Kozarac and its surroundings into the most horrifying drama from which many shall not emerge. Unfortunately, the victims shall also be those who are not to blame for the events happening in Potkozarje. RADE MUTIC: In the uniforms of the Green Berets, Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army overpowered the leadership, entered the town and forced the remaining dismembered formations of Muslim extremists to change clothes and put on dimije, Turkish trousers, and run to the forests of Kozara, while a considerable number of them have been captured. The information regarding the fighting in Hambarine, Kozarac, Kozarusa, and Kamicani is accessible only through the announcements of the Crisis Staff and the secretariat of information, which are being broadcast on an hourly basis on the local radio station. This way the public has been informed that a considerable number of hirelings from other parts of the country, who had already fought in the HOS Croatian Defence Forces and ZNG, National Guard Corps, have been fighting on the side of Muslim extremists, as well as a number of former officers and non-commissioned officers of the former Yugoslav People's Army, who've had the most responsible commanding positions and duties in those battles. The announcements also inform the public that the members of the Green Berets have used all means at their disposal to force local population into the fight until extinction, using the innocent local population, women, and children, as a human shield. The army, however, managed to pull part of the population out of the encirclement and house them, and also to put out the fire, which Muslim extremist had set around their own camp in the Kotlovaca mountain lodge. Once the resistance of the Muslim paramilitaries in Kozarac was quelled, many things became evident and many assumptions came true regarding the long and fateful preparations for the war of extermination into which Alija Izetbegovic first called up his own people, encouraged by the support of the numerous European and world administrators for churning out states. This way several large underground shelters and depots were discovered, equipped with radio stations and supplied with huge provisions of food and beverages, in addition to more than a ton of medication, sufficient for one year of warfare have not been on the market for several years. PREDRAG LAKETA: We are talking with Milomir Stakic, president of the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff. Mr. President, please describe to us the situation in the territory that is under your control. MILOMIR STAKIC: Well, I can tell you and the viewers that the whole territory of Prijedor municipality is under our control, which I can confirm following the liberation of Kozarac. The town, Serbian settlements and smaller enclaves with Muslim population have been under our control since the takeover on the 30th of April, and now, after the fall of Kozarac, the entire municipality is under our control. In Kozarac itself, the operation of "cleansing," as the military call it, is still going on, because those who have now stayed behind are the most extreme ones and the professionals. PREDRAG LAKETA: In the territory of Bosanska Gradiska municipality, 127 Muslim extremists have been caught who tried to escape to Croatia. In the settlement of Brdjani near Kozarac, there are about 1.000 members of the Green Berets and HOS who are sending word that they do not intend to surrender. All the locals who had illegally possessed weapons in the villages of Hrnici and Trnopolje handed them over to the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality except for the Trnopolje hamlet of Karalici. However, they are completely surrounded by the armed formations of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina so that the liberation of these places is soon expected.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The police is not the army."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The police is not the army. Dissatisfaction with the unit's commanding personnel was given as the pretext, but the real reasons surfaced later on. What did the policemen ask for, and what did the municipal authorities offer? Displeased with command of their unit, 127 members of a recently formed police battalion returned without authorisation from the Han Pijesak front on Thursday, the 17th of September. The very next day, Friday, the policemen met representatives of both the civilian and military municipal authorities and presented their demands, which were listed as eight items. This was the reason why the Municipal Council of the People's Defence planned to convene on Monday, take a position, and propose a solution. The same topic was the subject of yet another meeting on Tuesday, where many of the same people were present. The assembled policemen were informed about the fate of their demands by the president of the Assembly and the chairman of the executive board of Prijedor municipality. The president of the SDS municipal board, Dr. Milomir Stakic, was also present. The president of the municipal parliament explained to the policemen present that their first demand, an urgent session of the Municipal Assembly, was denied because the assembly does not discuss such matters. Actually, such matters are under the jurisdiction of the People's Defence Council, which, in any case, had immediately adopted a position. The second demand, placing all the policemen who deserted the front on stand-by status, was accepted. The third demand was to bring back all the rest of the police battalion from Han Pijesak. Stakic explained that such things were not under the jurisdiction of either the municipal civilian or military authorities because the decision on the formation of the police battalion had been issued by the Government of Republika Srpska and thus only the Cabinet could decide on its deployment to or its withdrawal from the front. A similar response was given concerning the fourth demand, that in future, no more than 10 per cent of the population fit for military service from Prijedor municipality should be assigned to areas of military operations in the former BH. Having remarked that such a decision exceeds the authority of the municipality, Milomir Stakic informed those present that the Prijedor civilian government had already addressed the republican government with the idea of having each municipality proportionately Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. represented in the military, based on the number of people of Serbian nationality in each municipality. The answer to the fifth demand, the removal of Captain Slijepcevic from his commanding post, was that the civilian authorities could not interfere with the staffing policy of the army, but that Colonel Arsic had been asked to reassess the commanding performance of the aforementioned officer. In their sixth demand, the policemen wanted to know why the prisoners from Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje had been released. Stakic indicated the two key reasons which had motivated the government in Pale to make such a decision: Pressure from international public opinion and official policy, and the steep cost of maintaining the prisons. The last demand, for a definition of the relationship between the civilian authorities, the army, and the police, received comment from the President of the Municipal Assembly. He said that legislative regulation already did exist, but that one should not expect from a state, such as Krajina, still in the process of forming, to resolve everything ideally from the start. Mico Kovacevic, president of the municipal government, supplemented the explanations given by Dr. Milomir Stakic, and this part of the meeting concluded with a proposal that the policemen who had deserted the front should choose one of the commanders at the Gradacac front and join his forces. In the course of the discussion and comments concerning positions taken by the municipal authority, a great deal of what had been obvious at first, but which was at the heart of the problem, which ended with their leaving Han Pijesak, suddenly became clear. The police is not the army, and should not go to the front but should stay to do its own job, this being a common opinion of the summoned members of the police battalion. Requests were heard for an explanation concerning the method of selection of which policemen were to stay in town and which were to be sent to the front. The opinion was also voiced that intolerance between the civilian and the military police, as well as between the police and the army, had already been smouldering for quite some time. The army apparently believed that the police had a privileged position and a less difficult and dangerous role in this war. A proposal cropped up that the Military Prosecutor should determine to what extent the decision to reassign the policemen to the army had been based on legal grounds. There was also an isolated opinion that the only way for these policemen to avoid being labelled as cowards and deserters was to return to Han Pijesak. Simo Miskovic, SDS leader, reminded those present that sacrifices had to be made for the Serbian cause and that there was no turning back from the road they had taken. In Prijedor, we will continue struggling to ensure that the burden of creating a new state is shared equally by all of its future citizens, said Miskovic, and appealed to the policemen not to allow their action to become a source of conflict among Serbs. Despite all the bitterness, distrust, and divisiveness in perceptions of the same problem, and significant disagreement concerning desires and ambitions even among the very policemen who had deserted the front, the meeting ended with a conclusion accepted by a close vote of those present. All 127 newly recruited soldiers of the Republika Srpska Army will turn to Han Pijesak."

In some of our documents it's translated as National Defence Council, in some the People's Defence Council, but I believe it's the same word in B/C/S that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Republika Srpska, ministry of internal affairs, Security Services Centre, Banja Luka, public security station, Prijedor. Report on the work of the Prijedor public security station during the last nine months of 1992. Prijedor, January 1993. A) creation of conditions for the functioning of the public security station. After the last multiparty elections, the SDA party assumed power in Prijedor and held, in addition to a large number of departments in the municipality, the most important positions in the public security station. In these circumstances, it proved very difficult to work on the organisational structure and preparation of personnel for the Serbian ministry of internal affairs. In view of the fact that the chief of the public security station in Prijedor and commander of the police station for the control and safety of traffic were both SDA people, these activities had to be covert and involve a very limited number of personnel. The work was carried out outside the station premises, often using the premises of the cultural centre in Cirkin Polje. The focus of the work was on the covert organisation and formation of "shadow" police stations and the arming and equipping of the personnel. In this manner, 13 police stations were established, with a total staff of about 1.500. Weapons, ammunition, and other materiel were acquired from various sources. The army was the primary source, and secretly, mostly at night, collected, transported, stored, and distributed to personnel for homekeeping and use. In these circumstances, and at a time when ethnic maps were being drafted which were placing Prijedor in Cazinska Krajina, activities were launched to prepare for a takeover by force. These activities gained momentum in April, and the actual date of the takeover was forced upon us by the Presidency of the then Socialist Republic of BH, when they issued the order to attack military installations and convoys. As a result, in the night between the 29th and 30th of April, 1992, following very detailed preparations and pursuant to the relevant decision of the Executive Committee of the Serbian municipality of Prijedor, an organised takeover of power was embarked upon. About 400 policemen assembled in the cultural centre of Cirkin Polje, and at 0400 hours they took control of the important sites in the town, which made possible the takeover of all leading functions in the Municipality, the municipal administration organs, and the important companies. After the takeover, all personnel of Croatian and Muslim ethnicity were summoned to interviews by the Chief of the SJB, and the option of signing declarations of allegiance to Republika Srpska was explained to them. They were all given a reasonable time limit, and in response to various requests - mostly from the police squads of Ljubija and of Kozarac - this time limit was extended twice. Additionally, interviews were also conducted with a number of Serbian members of the staff who had not been explicit enough in defining their future work engagement. Through these interviews, and talks with representatives of the local authorities and political leaders in areas populated mostly by Muslims and Croats, a process of differentiation took place so that it became evident who among the staff would be willing to sign a loyalty oath, and on the other hand, a number of Serbian staff were given a period of three or six months respectively, to show that they can work well and prove their worth in this new situation, which would secure their further engagement within the Public Security Station. These activities were interrupted by the outbreak of conflict, which started on the 22nd of May, 1992, when Muslim extremists attacked five military conscripts in the village of Hambarine, and gained intensity when a military convoy was attacked in the village of Jakupovici on the 24th of May, 1992. The conflict escalated and the policemen of Muslim ethnicity engaged fully on the Green Berets' side in the area of Kozarac, while many others who had been working in the town or in Ljubija and living in the areas populated primarily by non-Serbs made their services available to the enemy, or returned the equipment and weapons they had been issued by this Public Security Station. Three police employees signed the loyalty oath to Republika Srpska: one Ukranian and two persons from mixed marriages. These three are working in the Public Security Station in Prijedor to this very day. In addition to them, two police reservists of Croatian ethnicity signed the loyalty declaration, but one of them left his unit when it was fighting at Orasje and was subsequently discharged from the reserve police force. Until the 4th of April, 1992, a total of 453 people were employed in the Public Security Station in Prijedor: 145 on the active force and 308 on the reserve force. After the 4th of April, 1992, an organisational and functional restructuring of the Public Security Station was carried out with the active involvement of about 20 people, for the most part executives from the crime police and other services in the station. The number increased significantly in May, since with the takeover of the 29th of April, 1992, the covert mode of operation could be completely abandoned. The number of employees in the public security station of Prijedor fluctuated as follows: April: 145 active, 308 reserve, a total of 453 May: 145 active, 1.447 reserve, a total of 1.663 June: 148 active, 1.607 reserve, a total of 1.755 July: 153 active, 1.459 reserve, a total of 1.612 August: 171 active, 1.383 reserve, a total of 1.554 September: 177 active, 1.396 reserve, a total of 1.573 October: 180 active, 995 reserve, a total of 1.175 November: 185 active, 1.004 reserve, a total of 1.199 December: 184 active, 950 reserve, a total of 1.134 9 B) Participation of the members of the station in combat operations In our Municipality, combat operations commenced on the 22nd of May, 1992. Employees of this Station actively participated in these operations, primarily members of both the active and the reserve forces of the police. Combat activities were at their most intense in the areas of Kozarac, Kozarusa, Trnopolje, Kamicani, Rizvanovici, Biscani, Hambarine, Zecovi, Carakovo, Kurevo, Raljas, Cela, and the town of Prijedor itself. Eleven policemen were killed in combat, and 25 were lightly or seriously wounded. After these operations, the policemen engaged in intensive mopping-up activities, apprehending and debriefing certain individuals who could be connected to enemy activity in this area. Once the situation stabilised and the focus of combat shifted to other areas, police officers were dispatched to other battlefields, including: Kotor Vares, between the 24th of August and the 24th of September, 1992, 5 policemen. Below there is a sign. It's an "X." It reads as follows: Radenko Djapa on the 30th of April, 1992; Rajko Bilbija on 9th of May, 1992; Zeljko Gnjatovic on 30th of May; Dusko Lukic on the 30th of May; Mladen Vlacina on the 30th of May; Branko Djuricic on the 30th of May; Dario Davidovic on the 31st of May; Borislav Zujic, the 23rd of July; Milan Curguz on the 23rd of July; Milenko Gojic on 23rd of July; and Milenko Katana on 10th August, 1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the purposes of the transcript, it should be fixed that this is a footnote to the sentence saying that 11 policemen were killed in combat. I think we can proceed immediately on page 5, to the last paragraph, starting with "three collection centres."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4 of the B/C/S version. "Three collection centres were established in the territory of our municipality, that is, Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Omarska. Several thousands people passed through these centres, and about 6.000 informative interviews were conducted with them. Until the 21st of August, 1992, 187 police employees were involved in guard duties in these centres. Except for Trnopolje, all other reception centres were dismantled on the 21st of August, 1992, as there were no further security requirements for them. The Trnopolje reception centre, however, remained in place until November. In addition to women and children, there was a large concentration of Muslim men fit for military service there, including persons who had spent some time in Omarska and Keraterm because of their direct or indirect involvement in armed rebellion. As several convoys were organised for the transportation of these persons in the direction of Skender Vakuf, Bugojno, Karlovac, and Gradiska, our policemen took part in the escort and security details provided for the convoys. The following data reveal how important the participation of policemen employees and other authorised employees of the Public Security Station in Prijedor was for the combat operations: - 2 active and 11 reserve policemen were killed, or a total of 13 - 5 active and 20 reserve policemen were seriously wounded, or a total of 25 - 6 active and 36 reserve policemen were lightly wounded, or a total of 42. Total casualties: 13 active and 67 reserve policemen, a total of 80.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
